docs.title: Architecture Notes: How It All Works
docs.text:
This doc is a continuous work in progress.

This serves as the rough architecture guide for how the whole thing works if you're curious.

There are four core components in the Tartarus ecosystem:

  1. The Lock (Firmware): ESP32-S3 firmware written in Rust managing physical locking state, hardware security (Infineon Optiga Trust M or software fallback), display rendering via embedded-graphics, and local Bluetooth LE / USB serial interfaces.
  2. The Coordinator: Spring Boot + Kotlin backend providing REST APIs, MQTT messaging, hardware attestation verification, and WebSocket session management.
  3. The Web Application: Modern Angular application built with Spartan UI and Tailwind primitives at Tartarus, supporting in-browser Web Serial flashing, serial command dispatch, BLE management, and contract administration.
  4. Overlord & Bot Platform: Automated agent and bot services communicating over duplex WebSockets with author ownership for reactive lock automation and social interactions (e.g. Bluesky).

The "center" of the system is the Coordinator. The locks need somewhere to send and receive updates, process commands, etc. When they startup they check their local configuration and go through these steps:

docs.title: Cryptography
docs.text:
Almost every entity in the system has a public and private keypair.

Going into the details of a asymmetric cryptography is way beyond the scope of this doc. That being said:

  • All keys use curve secp256r1.
  • All public keys are represented in compressed form.
  • All hashes are calculated with sha256.
  • All signatures are to be in raw format, not DER.
  • All symmetric cryptography is aes-256-gcm.
  • All password that need to be verified are stored with Scrypt and params: 16384, 8, 1, 32.
  • Where HKDF is used, we populate the info field with the task at hand.
  • All ByteArrays are encoded with Base64 unless they are meant to be in a URL in which case we use URL-safe Base64.
  • Online keys (SafetyKey) are stored as PKCS8 since they aren't transmitted.

docs.title: SignedMessage
docs.text:
All the commands and contracts are implemented as SignedMessage. A SignedMessage is a flatbuffer with a signed payload. So when you make a contract you generate the entire Contract flatbuffer, calculate a hash of the whole table, sign that, and then attach the signature to the outer-wrapper of the SignedMessage.

Every entity that receives or forwards a SignedMessage will check the signature and reject the message if it fails to pass.

docs.title: Commands, Counters & Serial Numbers
docs.text:
All the commands after a Contract is accepted are to include a counter value. In order for a SignedMessage to be valid the counter value in the message has to be greater than or equal to the current counter in the lock. This is designed to prevent message replay (Someone trying to use an unlock code twice).

All commands also have to include both their own unique serial number and the serial number of the contract they are issued under. If the contract serial number in a message doesn't match the current contract it will be rejected. This prevents one person's messages from being used on a different lock.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
The hash of a flatbuffer has to also include the vtable of the message. Because the format essentially uses "pointers" in the format, all of those pointers also have to be covered- and those are the vtable. You'll see code like this almost anywhere a signature is needed:

builder.Finish(contract_offset)
bytes = builder.Output()

start = bytes[0]
contract_start = bytes[start]
vtable_start = start - contract_start
hash = hashlib.sha256(bytes[vtable_start:]).digest()
signature = signer.sign(hash)contract_start = bytes[start]
vtable_start = start - contract_start
hash = hashlib.sha256(bytes[vtable_start:]).digest()
signature = signer.sign(hash)

docs.title: Signature Format
docs.text: Signatures need to be raw r + s values, not DER encoded. This was an early design decision to minimize the size of SignedMessage tables so they would help fit inside scannable QR code blocks. The downside is most verification libraries like BouncyCastle want signatures in DER format so you'll need to convert them around.

docs.title: SignedEvent & Unified Telemetry
docs.text:
The lock generates cryptographically signed events for the coordinator, web admin sessions, and any authorized bots listed on a contract. They are similar in structure to SignedMessage, carrying a signed payload with common metadata and timestamps.

The events in the contract lifecycle and telemetry system are:

  • Accept - This event is emitted after the contract has been confirmed in the hardware.
  • Lock - The lock was locked via command from the coordinator or a bot.
  • Unlock - The lock was unlocked via command.
  • LocalLock - The lock button on the face of the lock was used. Only emits if temporary unlocking is allowed.
  • LocalUnlock - The unlock button on the face of the lock was used. Only emits if temporary unlocking is allowed.
  • Release - The contract was released and confirmed in hardware.
  • Abort - The contract was aborted via a designated SafetyKey.
  • EmergencyUnlock - The contract was unlocked via an emergency unlock command.
  • StartedUpdate - Telemetry emitted on lock boot announcing firmware version, lock state, and contract status.
  • PeriodicUpdate - Heartbeat telemetry published periodically while online. Bots with receive_events permissions will receive these periodic updates too.

docs.title: Contract structure
docs.text:
Contracts are pretty straight forward:

table Contract {
  serial_number: ushort;
  public_key: [ubyte];
  bots: [Bot];
  terms: string;
  // If true, subject can freely cycle the lock.
  is_temporary_unlock_allowed: bool;
}

Notes:

  • The serial number is randomly generated by the author.
  • The public_key is the author's public key. All future commands will need to be signed by this key.
  • The bots vector identifies which bots are allowed to participate in this contract.
  • The terms string is just an unstructured string. It can include whatever you want. None of the core bits of the system will try and interpret this field.
  • Lastly, should temporary unlocks be allowed. If this is true the buttons on the lock face will work, otherwise they won't.

docs.title: Bots & Permissions
docs.text:
Only bots listed on the contract body will be able to receive events. Events are published by the lock to isolated per-lock MQTT topics (tartarus/{lock_id}/events), and the coordinator filters and fans them out to authorized bots over duplex WebSockets. Bots will also receive periodic updates if they have event permissions.

Additionally, bots have four possible permission settings:

  • receive_events - Whether or not SignedEvent messages will be generated at their appropriate point in the lifecycle. If this is false no events will be sent to the bot.
  • can_unlock - If this is true the bot can sign an UnlockCommand and it will be accepted.
  • can_lock - Same as unlock but for lock.
  • can_release - If this is true the bot can end the contract.

docs.title: Lock Startup
docs.text:
What happens on lock startup:

  • Send StartedUpdate from the unified event.fbs flatbuffers. If the coordinator has never heard from this lock before, it creates a new LockSession. The update includes the lock's public key material, whether it started with an active contract, the firmware version, and the current lock state.
  • Receive a CoordinatorConfiguration message potentially updating the lock's local configuration or toggling experimental firmware features.
  • In the pre-1.2.0 world, we had scaffolding for OTA updates (GetLatestFirmwareRequest). The problem is that the Adafruit Reverse TFT Feather only has 4MB of flash, which became unworkable as firmware features grew. However, modern in-browser Web Serial flashing (/updater) obviated the need for OTA anyway, allowing the partition table to be standardized with a larger application partition and 24 KB NVS.
  • Authenticate hardware security: The firmware uses a pluggable SecurityBackend architecture. For "official" hardware builds, an Infineon Optiga Trust M secure element module provides hardware-isolated keys and ECDSA signing; the coordinator cryptographically verifies the hardware certificate chain against Infineon Root CAs. The "official" build is an optional additional layer of security for those that want a slightly more oppressive experience—especially good for software people who know how things work! Homebrew builds run smoothly using the software security backend.

From there, it will publish a PeriodicUpdate event once a minute indefinitely (which is also forwarded to authorized bots).

docs.title: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) & Offline Storage
docs.text:
To support scenarios where Wi-Fi is intermittent or unavailable, the firmware incorporates local transport and buffering:

  • On-Board BLE GATT Server: An embedded BLE GATT server (ble_server.rs) allows direct interaction with the lock without requiring Wi-Fi. It uses challenge-response authentication over GATT characteristics for issuing commands, reading device status, and draining audit events.
  • Offline Ring Buffer: A 20-event circular buffer (event_buffer.rs) captures state changes (such as local lock/unlock toggles) when the lock is offline. Once Wi-Fi reconnects or a client connects over BLE, buffered events are automatically flushed and synced.

docs.title: LockSession
docs.text: A LockSession uniquely defines a particular Tartarus lock.

docs.title: LockUserSession
docs.text: This is an owner of a Tartarus lock logged into the website. You can simultaneously have a LockUserSession and an AuthorSession.

docs.title: AuthorSession
docs.text: This is someone logged into the website with a keypair image they generated and is authoring/managing contracts. You can simultaneously have a LockUserSession and an AuthorSession.

docs.title: AdminSession
docs.text: Admin users that have special, magical powers.

docs.title: SafetyKey
docs.text: A set of reserved online keys that can sign Abort messages. Only AdminSession users can use SafetyKeys.

docs.title: Bill of Materials
docs.text: In order to build the lock you will need:

docs.title: Mandatory parts
docs.text:
• Adafruit ESP32-S3 Reverse TFT Feather - 4MB Flash, 2MB PSRAM, STEMMA QT. Homebrew versions are totally welcome and don't limit your features.
  • STEMMA QT / Qwiic JST SH 4-Pin Cable - 50mm Long
  • Micro servo - TowerPro SG92R - You can also use any generic SG90/SG92 form factor servo.
  • 7x Socket Head Cap Screw: M2-0.4 Thread Size, 8 mm Lg, Std, Black Oxide, Steel, Class 12.9, 100 PK
  • 7x Hex Nut: M2-0.40 Thread, 4 mm Hex Wd, 1.6 mm Hex Ht, Steel, Class 8, Zinc Plated, 100 PK
  • Adhesive: 2-part Epoxy is strongly recommended for a robust and tamper-resistant seal. (Hot glue can be used if you want some margin of error during prototyping, but 2-part epoxy is recommended for permanent assembly).

docs.title: Hardware Security Module (For Official Builds)
docs.text: • Optiga Trust M Breakout (available from Adafruit or DigiKey). Connected via STEMMA QT / Qwiic. Required if you want an "official" build with hardware-backed cryptographic identity and badge on the coordinator. Homebrew builds without this module use the built-in software SecurityBackend.

docs.title: Legacy / Optional parts
docs.text: • Tiny Code Reader from Useful Sensors - Notice: We now explicitly advise against using the QR code reader, and updated shape files for the build will not include a slot for it. Wi-Fi setup and device management are now handled over Web Serial USB or Bluetooth LE.

docs.title: Optional, but good to have
docs.text:
• 3M VHB Tape (or high-strength double-sided foam mounting tape) — Used to mount the Optiga Trust M breakout board firmly to the inside of the case.
  • Loctite Threadlocker Blue - Makes the lock more tamper resistant.
  • Tiny cable tie
  • 4mm Nut driver - Definitely makes tightening the nuts easier, but far from necessary. Also you probably want a magnetized one, but this is what I have.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• Soldering iron
  • Technical screwdriver (T6 bit)
  • Tiny technical flathead screwdriver or razor blade (used to lift the retaining tabs on the servo connector to swap 3V3 and GND pins)

docs.title: 3D Files
docs.text:
You can get the full kit of parts here: Full kit

I personally use Prusa slicer + the Prusa MINI+ for most builds. I use organic supports, 15% infill, and the 0.20mm SPEED profile. Feel free to adjust as necessary. I recommend printing with PLA.

docs.title: Step 2: Solder headers to ESP32-S3
docs.text:

Use a pair of pliers and break off 3 headers from the full strip that comes with the ESP32-S3.

You'll solder these headers (short-side through top) across 3V, GND, and A0. See picture. Also check out the pinout guide from Adafruit.

docs.title: Step 3: Flash the firmware
docs.text:
[!TIP] Recommended Method: Almost everyone should just be using the in-browser Web Serial Flasher. It connects over Web Serial (in Chrome, Edge, or Opera) to automatically flash the latest official signed release, configure partitions, and report status without installing Rust or command-line developer tools.

Important: If you are flashing the official signed release, please review the Signed Firmware & Secure Boot v2 guide before flashing. Enabling Secure Boot v2 is an irreversible 1-way physical change to the microcontroller eFuses.

docs.title: Manual Flashing via Command Line (Developers)
docs.text:
If you are developing custom firmware or flashing locally from source:

`

Hold down D0 and press Reset. Build and flash the firmware with:

cargo build --release

espflash flash --monitor --partition-table partitions.csv target/xtensa-esp32s3-espidf/release/tartarus-firmware

If it looks like it succeeded but says "Waiting for download" you just need to reset it one more time.

You should see the boot screen followed by "Needs configuration."

We do this now because we need the firmware to calibrate the servo.

docs.title: Step 4: Assemble servo bracket
docs.text:
• 2x 2mm screws
  • 2x hex nuts
  • 1x mounting bracket
  • 1x SG92 servo (with single-ended horn, and small screw that came with it)

`

docs.title: Step 5: Wire servo to ESP32-S3 (Repin Servo Connector)
docs.text:
[!IMPORTANT] No Jumper Wires: In the newer revision of the hardware, internal clearance is tight and there is not enough space to accommodate female-to-male jumper wires. We do not recommend using jumper wires. Instead, repin the servo's 3-pin Molex connector directly so it plugs straight onto the board headers.

The ESP32-S3 board pinout across the 3 soldered headers is 3V, GND, and A0 (Signal), whereas standard servo wiring is GND (brown/black), 3V (red), and Signal (yellow/orange).

To swap the pin assignment directly on the servo connector: 1. Use a tiny technical flathead screwdriver or razor blade to gently lift the small plastic retaining tabs on the servo's Molex housing for the 3V (red) and GND (brown/black) pins. 2. Slide the red and brown/black crimp terminals out of the plastic housing (leave the signal wire untouched). 3. Swap their positions so 3V is on the outside, matching the ESP32-S3's 3V, GND, A0 pinout. 4. Slide them back into the housing until the plastic tabs click securely into place. 5. Plug the repinned connector directly onto the 3-pin header on the ESP32-S3.

Connect USB power to the ESP32-S3 and you will probably hear a quick buzz. The servo is now in the "down" angle position so we can mount the horn.

docs.title: Step 6: Mount the horn
docs.text:
`

Mount the horn at 6 as if it were a clock. Connect power back to the ESP32-S3 and make sure the servo starts at 6. Toggle the lock on the second screen (D2 to change screen and then by pressing D1, the middle button). It should freely rotate to a 3 o'clock position and back. If it does, use the small-sized screw and mount the horn permanently. Try not to rotate the horn while tightening.

docs.title: Step 8: Wire and mount Optiga Trust M (Official Builds)

• Optiga Trust M Breakout
  • STEMMA QT / Qwiic JST SH 4-Pin Cable (50mm)

Connect the Optiga Trust M breakout to the ESP32-S3 board using the 50mm STEMMA QT cable. Cut a small piece of 3M VHB tape and affix the back of the breakout board securely to the inside wall of the enclosure, ensuring the board and cable stay completely clear of the sliding tray and servo arm. The orientation doesn't matter but I personally arrange it so the silkscreen printed shackle points toward the tray.

docs.text: Plug it in and cycle the lock. When you're satisfied it's all working make the wire connections permanent with 2-part epoxy.

docs.text:
`

I use 2-part epoxy on the left sill, the right sill, and across the front where all the technical parts are mounted. If you're using hot glue for temporary testing, be sure wherever you apply it doesn't interfere with the tray sliding in and out.

In order to get the best seal I recommend leaving a heavy weight on it while it cures. I have a tupperware full of change for this. Give it an hour or two.

docs.title: V 1.2.0
docs.text:
Release 1.2.0 is a comprehensive release spanning the entire Tartarus ecosystem since commit d82e1d6d. This release introduces hardware-backed security via Infineon Optiga Trust M, a streamlined custom embedded-graphics display engine, an overhaul of the event and protocol architecture, a modernized WebSocket-based bot platform, Spartan UI frontend redesign, and end-to-end hardware attestation and provisioning.

[!WARNING] Breaking Change — Firmware Upgrade Required: Because this release fundamentally changes the underlying FlatBuffers protocol (migrating lifecycle and status telemetry such as StartedUpdate and PeriodicUpdate directly into the unified Event schema) and overhauls how bots communicate and interact (transitioning from REST polling to a WebSocket-based author ownership architecture), this is a breaking change across the entire ecosystem. Operating on the Tartarus network going forward requires upgrading physical locks to firmware 1.2.0 or higher; legacy firmware will not be able to process bot commands or dispatch telemetry to modern coordinators.

docs.title: Hardware Security & Secure Element
docs.text:
• SecurityBackend Architecture: Introduced a pluggable SecurityBackend abstraction trait in the firmware, decoupling core contract and cryptographic routines from underlying storage and crypto implementations.
  • Infineon Optiga Trust M Integration: Integrated native hardware security module support for the Infineon Optiga Trust M secure element, providing hardware-isolated private keys, ECDSA signing, and tamper-resistant cryptographic storage.
  • Software Fallback Backend: Retained a software-based SecurityBackend implementation for local development and hardware units lacking dedicated secure cryptoprocessors.
  • Hardware Factory Provisioning: Added a dedicated firmware factory provisioning command interface and soft provisioning modes for staging device identities, root certificates, and cryptographic keys.
  • Coordinator Hardware Verification: Implemented certificate chain validation in the coordinator to cryptographically verify hardware authenticity and attestation reports against official Infineon Root CAs.
  • Admin Provisioning Console: Added a web-based provisioning ingestion modal allowing administrators to inspect and verify hardware units over Web Serial.

docs.title: Firmware Architecture & Display Engine
docs.text:
• Embedded-Graphics Migration: Removed the Slint UI framework dependency in favor of a lean, custom display stack built on embedded-graphics (src/ui/mod.rs, components.rs, screens.rs, theme.rs, font.rs). This dramatically reduces flash footprint, eliminates runtime overhead, and prevents heap thrashing.
  • Typography & UI Components: Added raster font rendering with bundled DejaVuSans typography, standardized color themes, and dedicated screen layouts for status, lock state, Wi-Fi info, and QR presentation.
  • Display Optimizations: Cached QR code rendering to eliminate redraw latency, and added animated visual feedback indicators on unlock execution.
  • Main Thread Stack Expansion: Increased ESP32 main task stack size to 32 KB to safely handle deep cryptographic verification chains and large protocol payloads.
  • Firmware Version Reporting: Updated the firmware to self-report its semantic version during initialization and periodic updates, ingested directly into coordinator lock sessions.

docs.title: Protocol & Unified Event Model
docs.text:
• Unified Event Telemetry: Migrated StartedUpdate and PeriodicUpdate from message payloads into first-class FlatBuffers Event definitions (dc50673), creating a single unified pipeline for device status, lock state transitions, and audit logs.
  • Emergency Unlock: Added end-to-end protocol support for emergency unlock operations across FlatBuffers schemas, firmware state machines, and coordinator event services.
  • Safety Key Signature Validation: Cryptographically enforced that AbortCommand and ResetCommand payloads can only be authorized by designated SafetyKeys.
  • Bot Permission Enforcement: Implemented strict capability authorization checks (can_lock, can_unlock, can_release) for incoming bot commands and restricted outbound event dispatching exclusively to authorized bots.
  • Isolated Per-Lock Topics: Standardized MQTT topic hierarchies to per-lock paths (tartarus/{lock_id}/...) for commands, updates, and event streams, preventing cross-lock topic interference.
  • Multi-Chunk Message Reassembly: Replaced legacy message assemblers with a robust, per-topic MessageAssembler capable of safely reassembling interleaved multi-part payloads.

docs.title: Overlord & Bot Ecosystem
docs.text:
• WebSocket Bot Architecture: Transitioned the Overlord bot platform from REST polling to a high-throughput, duplex WebSocket architecture with explicit author ownership.
  • Simplified Bot Core: Streamlined BotComponent and bot implementations (SimpleProxyBot, SuperBot, AnnouncerBot), making the codebase significantly easier to extend, test, and maintain.
  • Conversational Intent Engine: Refactored the natural conversation intent parsing pipeline into modular, maintainable intent handlers (ProxyLockIntent, ProxyUnlockIntent, ProxyReleaseIntent, ProxyContractIntent).
  • Dependency & Protocol Updates: Updated Bluesky social integration dependencies and modernized bot integration test suites.

docs.title: Coordinator Backend
docs.text:
• Hardware Attestation Services: Added services to validate device certificates, challenge-response nonces, and hardware identity tokens.
  • Lock Session Enhancements: Added tracking of active firmware versions across lock sessions and direct navigation links from contract management views to corresponding lock sessions.
  • Admin Event Subscriptions: Introduced dedicated WebSocket admin sessions with token authentication and live administrative event broadcasting.
  • Serial Acknowledgments: Added support for processing manual command acknowledgments received out-of-band via USB serial.
  • Persistence & Security Hardening: Corrected JPA @OneToMany entity mappings, enforced MariaDB dialect compatibility in test runners, safeguarded JWT filter chains against duplicate executions, and expanded nonce cache sizes.

docs.title: Web Frontend & Modernization
docs.text:
• Spartan UI Migration: Modernized the Angular application by transitioning components to Spartan UI (spartan.ng) and Tailwind CSS primitives (hlm dialogs, sheets, cards, tables, badges, buttons, tooltips, sonner toasts, and spinners).
  • View Redesigns: Completely overhauled key views including "My Lock", Contract Creator, Lock User Contract Details, Author Contract View, and Lock Sessions.
  • In-Browser Web Serial Flashing: Built an integrated Web Serial firmware updater (updater.component.ts) capable of flashing devices directly from the browser with partition awareness and baud-rate selection.
  • Web Serial Command Terminal: Added direct "Send via serial" capabilities onto command cards with STDIN Base64 encoding.
  • BLE Device Management: Added interactive BLE controls for querying device status, inspecting the on-device event queue, and draining buffered offline events.
  • Angular Upgrades: Upgraded frontend core dependencies through Angular 20, 21, and 22, along with Angular CDK 21.

docs.title: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) & Offline Storage
docs.text:
• On-Board BLE GATT Server: Implemented an embedded BLE GATT server (ble_server.rs) enabling direct local interaction without active Wi-Fi.
  • GATT Challenge-Response Auth: Secured BLE management characteristics with challenge-response cryptographic authentication.
  • Offline Ring Buffer: Implemented an in-memory 20-event ring buffer (event_buffer.rs) that preserves audit logs when Wi-Fi is disconnected and automatically flushes on reconnection or BLE drain.

docs.title: System, Security & Flashing Tooling
docs.text:
• Secure Boot v2: Integrated Secure Boot v2 configuration with ECDSA image signatures for bootloader and application verification.
  • Partition Layout Optimization: Standardized non-volatile storage (NVS) at 24 KB and retired legacy OTA partition schemes to maximize app flash space.
  • Framework Upgrade: Upgraded underlying firmware framework to ESP-IDF 5.5.4.
  • Backup & Diagnostic Utilities: Added backup_nvs.sh for preserving cryptographic identity across flashes, automated manifest generation (firmware.json), and comprehensive protocol documentation (PROTOCOL.md).

docs.title: Reliability & Bug Fixes
docs.text:
• Contract Memory Corruption: Fixed an issue where loading a secondary contract corrupted in-memory command counters and triggered system panics.
  • Large Contract NVS Deserialization: Fixed contract buffer limits in NVS reads (expanded from 1 KB to 4 KB) to ensure large contracts load reliably without boot failure.
  • LLVM Xtensa LTO Instruction Selection: Resolved compiler crash (XtensaISD::PCREL_WRAPPER) under link-time optimization (opt-level = "z") by extracting MQTT closures into non-inlined worker functions.
  • Heap Allocation Reductions: Reworked struct layouts across LockCtx and network workers to eliminate unnecessary dynamic memory allocations.
  • Asynchronous Wi-Fi Reconnection: Reworked WifiManager connection routines with exponential backoff and asynchronous DHCP handling.

docs.title: V 1.1.1
docs.text: Release 1.1.1 represents a major architectural modernization and hardening of the Tartarus firmware since commit d82e1d6d. Highlights include a transition to Slint for the on-device user interface, on-board BLE GATT server integration, offline event buffering, Secure Boot support, and numerous protocol security enhancements.

docs.title: User Interface & Display
docs.text:
• Migration to Slint UI: Replaced the legacy embedded-graphics screen engine with a modern declarative Slint UI framework (ui/app.slint), retiring the old static screen modules (qr_screen, lock_state_screen, wifi_info_screen, overlays).
  • Unlock Visual Feedback: Added an animated flashing screen indicator on unlock execution.
  • QR Display Optimization: Cached QR code rendering to eliminate display redraw lag and prevent screen tearing on large payload transfers.

docs.title: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)
docs.text:
• On-Board BLE GATT Server: Implemented a full BLE GATT server (ble_server.rs) enabling direct communication with the lock without requiring Wi-Fi.
  • GATT Authentication & Controls: Added challenge-response authentication over BLE and GATT characteristics for querying device status, issuing commands, and inspecting/draining the event queue.

docs.title: Event System & Offline Storage
docs.text:
• Dedicated Per-Lock Event Queues: Refactored event publishing so locks stream state updates and notifications directly to their own dedicated topics for coordinator fanout.
  • Offline Event Ring Buffer: Added a 20-event in-memory ring buffer (event_buffer.rs) that captures and preserves audit events when the lock is offline, flushing them automatically upon reconnection or via BLE.

docs.title: System, Partitions & Security
docs.text:
• ESP-IDF 5.5.4 Upgrade: Upgraded core framework and hal dependencies to ESP-IDF 5.5.4.
  • Secure Boot Support: Integrated Secure Boot v2 configuration (sdkconfig.defaults.secureboot) with ECDSA signature verification for bootloader and firmware images.
  • Partition Table Rework: Deprecated and removed legacy OTA partitions to maximize app binary space; standardized NVS storage at 24 KB.
  • Web Serial Flashing: Added distribution builds (build_firmware_dist.sh) and manifest generation (firmware.json) enabling in-browser flashing over Web Serial.
  • NVS Backup Utility: Added backup_nvs.sh to safely backup and restore lock credentials, identity, and contracts across firmware flashes.
  • USB Serial Command Input: Added STDIN command reading over USB with Base64 armoring for local recovery and diagnostics.

docs.title: Protocol & Security Hardening
docs.text:
• Emergency Unlock: Added support for protocol-level Emergency Unlock commands across FlatBuffers schemas and internal contract handlers.
  • Safety Key Enforcement: Enforced cryptographic validation ensuring only designated SafetyKeys can sign AbortCommand and ResetCommand payloads.
  • Bot Permission Checks: Enforced strict authorization checks (can_lock, can_unlock, can_release) on incoming bot commands and restricted outbound event dispatching to authorized bots.
  • Key Parsing: Hardened SEC1 elliptic curve public key parsing and challenge-response handling.

docs.title: Networking & MQTT
docs.text:
• Aggressive Asynchronous Wi-Fi: Overhauled WifiManager with an asynchronous connection strategy, better scan handling, DHCP delay accommodation, and aggressive reconnection logic.
  • Standardized MQTT Topics: Standardized per-lock topic paths for commands, updates, and event streams.
  • Multi-Chunk Message Reassembly: Replaced firmware-specific assemblers with a generalized MessageAssembler isolated per MQTT topic to prevent interleaved packet corruption.
  • Low-Latency Publisher: Reduced MQTT publisher worker polling latency from 2000 ms to 50 ms for responsive command acknowledgments.

docs.title: Fixes & Performance
docs.text:
• Contract Command Counter Corruption: Fixed a bug where loading a secondary contract could corrupt the command counter in memory or cause a panic.
  • Large Contract Serialization: Resolved issues where large contracts could be stored in NVS but failed to re-load or caused boot panics.
  • Boot State Sync: Fixed boot order in LockCtx to ensure NVS contract state is restored prior to the initial StartedUpdate announcement.
  • LLVM Xtensa LTO Crash: Fixed a release-mode compiler crash (XtensaISD::PCREL_WRAPPER) under opt-level = "z" by refactoring MQTT worker closures into non-inlined routines.
  • Heap Allocation Reduction: Reworked memory layouts across LockCtx, verifiers, and network services to significantly reduce dynamic heap allocations.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text: [!IMPORTANT] Before You Flash: If you plan to install the official production firmware, please read the Signed Firmware & Secure Boot v2 section before flashing your hardware. Enabling Secure Boot v2 permanently burns key hashes into physical eFuses inside the microcontroller and cannot be undone.

docs.title: Getting Connected
docs.text:
The primary step to completing setup is configuring network connectivity on the lock.

There are several ways to configure and manage your lock:

docs.title: 1. Web Serial Console (Recommended for Modern Builds)
docs.text:
If your lock does not have a QR camera module, you can configure Wi-Fi and manage setup directly over USB using the Web Serial Console:

  • Plug your lock into your computer via USB-C.
  • Open the console in Chrome or Edge and click Connect (115200 baud).
  • You can view real-time boot logs, monitor Wi-Fi association and DHCP status, or enter Base64-armored configuration commands directly into STDIN.

docs.title: 2. Wi-Fi QR Code (Legacy Builds with Camera)
docs.text:
If your lock is built with the Useful Sensors Tiny Code Reader module:

  • Use the Wi-Fi helper in the web app to generate a credentials QR code. (All processing occurs locally in your browser).
  • Alternatively, generate a WPA3 Wi-Fi QR code using iOS/macOS Passwords app or Windows 11.
  • Hold the code in front of the camera module until the lock reads it and connects.

docs.title: 3. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)
docs.text:
The lock runs an on-board BLE GATT server (ble_server.rs). Using a compatible BLE browser or client:

  • Pair with the lock over BLE using challenge-response authentication.
  • Query device health, inspect buffered offline events, and issue management commands locally without active Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Verifying it worked
docs.text:
Once the lock is online it will try and connect to the default message broker at wss://tartarus-mqtt.subjugated.club:4447/mqtt. If it succeeds it will download a configuration blob containing everything it needs to create login credentials for you.

Give it a reset and a scannable QR code should be on the display after it boots.

docs.title: Signed Firmware & Secure Boot v2
docs.text: Tartarus offers official production firmware releases cryptographically signed with ESP32-S3 Secure Boot v2. You can flash these signed builds directly in your browser using the Web Serial Updater.

docs.title: What is Secure Boot v2?
docs.text: Secure Boot v2 creates a cryptographic chain of trust anchored directly in the physical silicon of the ESP32-S3 microcontroller. On power-up, the read-only hardware ROM verifies the cryptographic signature of the bootloader before executing it; the bootloader then verifies the signature of the application firmware image before executing the lock operating system.

docs.title: What are the Benefits?
docs.text:
• Absolute Tamper Resistance: Nobody—including the lock owner or anyone with physical access to the device—can flash modified, patched, or backdoored firmware to force open the servo, bypass contract counters, or dump encryption keys.
  • Hardware Anti-Rollback: Hardware eFuse counters enforce version monotonicity, preventing downgrades to older firmware versions that may have had bugs.
  • Locked Hardware Debugging: Secure Boot permanently disables hardware JTAG debugging pins and enables Secure ROM Download Mode. This prevents attackers from dumping flash or SRAM contents over USB serial.
  • Coordinator Attestation: Allows the lock to cryptographically prove its authenticity to the coordinator, granting verified status and hardware badges.
  • Psychological & Contract Integrity: For software engineers and tech-savvy lock owners who know how microcontrollers work, knowing that the lock cannot be hacked or reflashed with custom scripts provides true psychological peace of mind and an uncompromising, binding lock experience.

docs.title: ⚠️ Permanent 1-Way Process (Cannot Be Undone)
docs.text:
[!CAUTION] Enabling Secure Boot v2 is 100% PERMANENT and IRREVERSIBLE.

When the ESP32-S3 boots a Secure Boot v2 bootloader for the first time, it permanently burns the public key digest into one-time programmable (OTP) physical eFuses inside the silicon chip.

  • eFuses cannot be cleared, erased, or reset. Once burned, there is no factory reset command, no JTAG unbricking method, and no recovery utility on earth that can reverse it.
  • From that moment on, the ESP32-S3 hardware ROM will ONLY boot bootloaders and firmware images cryptographically signed by the official private release key.
  • If you flash unsigned code, custom homebrew firmware, or other hobbyist platforms (such as CircuitPython or Arduino), the hardware ROM will reject the signature and refuse to boot, entering an immediate boot loop.
  • You can still install official updates! The bootloader is built in reflashable mode, meaning future official releases from subjugated.club (e.g., v1.2.0, v1.2.1) can be flashed seamlessly over the in-browser Web Serial updater or command line.

If you plan to repurpose your ESP32-S3 board for other general electronics projects in the future, do not flash the signed release or enable Secure Boot v2. If you want a dedicated, hardened lock that cannot be defeated by serial reflashing, Secure Boot v2 is strongly recommended.

docs.title: Lock User Guide - So You Want Someone To Hold Your Keys
Step 1: Complete Build + Setup
docs.text: Make sure your lock is assembled, powered, and connected to the network (or accessible via Web Serial / BLE).

docs.title: Step 2: Login
docs.text: Scan the QR code displayed on the screen of the lock (or use the credentials generated during initial setup). This opens an authenticated LockUserSession on Tartarus, bringing you to the My Lock dashboard.

docs.title: Step 3: Share Links & Tokens
docs.text:
In the "My Lock" dashboard, you have two invitation links:

  • Share Link (s-...): When your author writes a contract with this link, you receive an invitation in your dashboard with full details. You have the choice to accept or reject it.
  • Total Control Link (tc-...): If you give someone your Total Control link, any contract they submit will bypass manual confirmation and be sent directly to the hardware for automatic acceptance.

docs.title: Step 4: Review and Accept Contracts
docs.text:
When a contract proposal arrives under a Share token, review: * The contract terms and duration. * Whether temporary unlocking via the physical lock buttons is permitted. * Which automated bots are attached, and what permissions they have (can_lock, can_unlock, can_release, receive_events).

If you agree, click Accept Contract. The lock physically engages and seals.

docs.title: Step 5: Operating the Lock & Offline Buffering
docs.text:
• Temporary Unlocks: If allowed by your contract, you can navigate to the lock screen on the physical device (press D2 to cycle screens) and press D1 (the middle button) to toggle between locked and unlocked.
  • Offline Event Ring Buffer: If your Wi-Fi is temporarily offline, you can still cycle temporary unlocks. The firmware records these actions in an on-board 20-event ring buffer, which automatically drains and syncs to the coordinator and author as soon as Wi-Fi reconnects or via BLE.
  • Emergency Safeguards: If an unexpected emergency occurs or connectivity is permanently lost, contracts can be released using the Emergency Unlock protocol or aborted by an administrator using an offline SafetyKey.

docs.title: Author Guide - So You Want To Hold Some Keys
Step 1: Get A Keypair
docs.text:
Generate a keypair using the key generator. This keypair is how you log in and what the software will use to sign all your contracts and commands.

Do not share it. Especially with your sub. It's functionally a master private key. Anyone with this image or key file can release or unlock a contract.

Protect it. Treat it like a physical key your sub handed you. If you lose it you'll need an administrator with a designated SafetyKey to abort the contract.

docs.title: Step 2: Login
docs.text: Go to Tartarus Login and select Author Login. Upload or drag and drop your saved keypair image/file. The browser verifies the key locally and establishes an authenticated AuthorSession.

docs.title: Step 3: Get A Token From Your Sub
docs.text:
Every sub has two links: the "share" link and the "total control" link. The "share" token starts with s- and the total control token starts with tc-.

  • An s- token lets you write a contract and send it to your sub for review and accept/reject.
  • A tc- token lets you write a contract and issue it directly to hardware. If the lock is online, it will auto-accept it.

The website will clearly identify which token type you are viewing. When you load the link, it becomes a KnownToken saved to your account. In the modernized Spartan UI dashboard, known tokens are displayed as cards under "Lock sessions". You can label them to keep track of who they belong to, or delete them when a session is finished.

docs.title: Step 4: Write A Contract
docs.text:
Using the Contract Creator: * Set contract terms and duration. * Configure whether temporary unlocks via physical lock buttons are permitted. * Attach automated bots with granular permissions (can_lock, can_unlock, can_release, and receive_events).

Once submitted, the contract is signed with your author key and dispatched to the lock.

docs.title: Step 5: Managing the Lock & Serial Fallback
docs.text:
From the Author Contract View, you can issue commands (Lock, Unlock, Release, or EmergencyUnlock).

[!TIP] Serial Command Fallback: If the lock is offline or experiencing network difficulties, command cards feature a Send via serial option. You can copy the Base64 command armored string and transmit it directly over USB serial via the Web Serial Console.

docs.title: Step 6: Release
docs.text: When the agreed terms are fulfilled, click Release Contract. The author key signs a ReleaseCommand and, upon confirmation from the lock, the contract is ended and the hardware unlocks.

docs.title: What is Tartarus?
docs.text: Tartarus is an open-source hardware lock system, primarily designed for chastity, but it could be used for anything. Think of it as an erotic application of modern cryptography.

docs.title: The Parts
docs.text:
The physical lock is an ESP32-S3 powered smart lock that communicates over Wi-Fi (MQTT), Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE GATT), and USB (Web Serial) for contract and lock management. You can place your keys in the lock, agree to terms online with your keyholder, and then have it remotely sealed and managed.

It's composed of the physical pieces (the actual physical lock you can build), the coordinator (for issuing commands, managing contracts, keys, and hardware verification), a network of automated bots connected via duplex WebSockets, and Overlord-exe (the Bluesky bot/interaction layer).

docs.title: What makes it different?
docs.text:
It brings a lot of BDSM dynamics into the online world. You can have people in far off locations manage your keys, give you tasks, have group accountability etc. The options are endless!

  • Remote keyholding
  • Engaging interaction directly in Bluesky (Overlord tasks)
  • More! :-)
